name: Alexandrite laser hair removal

card.summary: A 755 nm clinic laser for hair reduction, used mainly on lighter skin with dark hair; reduction, not total removal.
card.note: Hair reduction needs multiple sessions; light, grey or red hair responds poorly, and pigment changes are a recognised risk.

quick.overview:
Alexandrite lasers emit 755 nm light that melanin absorbs strongly, so they are used for dark hair. Clinics commonly use them for fast treatment of large areas on lighter skin tones.

Published comparisons find alexandrite among the more studied hair-removal lasers. Wikipedia describes a 2006 review that found roughly 67 to 72 percent reduction at six months across alexandrite, diode and IPL.
quick.mechanism: Selective photothermolysis: the light heats melanin in hair and follicle while skin is cooled, damaging actively growing follicles. Because only growing hairs respond, multiple sessions are typically scheduled.
quick.risks: Reported effects include redness, swelling, acne flares, burns and hyper- or hypopigmentation. Lighter hair responds poorly. The FDA defines "permanent" reduction as long-term stable reduction, not guaranteed removal.

lead: Alexandrite laser hair removal uses a 755 nm laser, absorbed by melanin, to reduce dark hair through selective photothermolysis. Wikipedia lists alexandrite among the standard hair-removal lasers alongside ruby, diode and Nd:YAG. [1]
The treatment works best on dark, coarse hair, and light, grey, red or fine hair respond poorly; multiple sessions are needed because lasers act on actively growing follicles. [1]
Alexandrite lasers also exist in picosecond and Q-switched forms used for tattoos and pigmented lesions, which are separate treatments. [2][3][4]
infobox: Wikipedia lists "all"; usually favoured for lighter skin
Often eight or more, spaced weeks apart

paras: Melanin is the main target chromophore; matching wavelength, pulse duration and fluence heats the follicle enough to disable it while epidermal cooling (contact cooling, cryogen spray or cold air) protects skin. [1]

Wikipedia reports that most people need at least eight sessions, spaced three to eight weeks apart, with touch-ups often needed. [1] It describes a 2006 review finding no significant short-term difference among alexandrite, diode and IPL (about 67 to 72 percent reduction at six months), with side effects in 9.5 percent for alexandrite versus 28.9 percent for diode and 15.3 percent for IPL. [1]

Common short-lived effects include itching, redness and swelling; acne flare-ups and discoloration are the most common serious effects, along with possible burns and infection. [1] A 1999 paper compared side effects of Q-switched Nd:YAG, long-pulsed ruby and alexandrite hair-removal lasers. [5]

Research on alexandrite lasers in the literature covers hair removal side effects [5], picosecond alexandrite treatment of tattoos [3][4], pigmented lesions in Asian patients [6], and Q-switched alexandrite for freckles and nevus of Ota [7][8]. Registered trials examine alexandrite lasers for hidradenitis suppurativa, acne scars and wrinkles. [9][10] Many of these concern uses other than hair removal.
